world_behind.title: The block begins
world_behind.text: This is Isaiah 2, the first of thirteen chapters Nephi copies without interruption. He kept the source's own heading, so the chapter opens by naming its author and subject. A reader moving from chapter 11 to chapter 12 changes centuries and countries in one line.

world_behind.title: Judah's boom years
world_behind.text: The oracle describes a kingdom with silver, gold, horses, chariots, and idols in quantity. Isaiah prophesied through a stretch of unusual prosperity for Judah, and the chapter treats the prosperity itself as the evidence: full treasuries, full stables, full shrines, and a people who bow to none of it.

world_behind.title: Soothsayers and strangers
world_behind.text: Verse 6 names two imports, foreign divination and pleasure in "the children of strangers" (v. 6). Small kingdoms between empires absorbed their neighbors' practices through trade and treaty. The complaint is dependence: the covenant people are described as replenished from somewhere other than their covenant.

world_behind.title: Tarshish and the sea
world_behind.text: Ships of Tarshish were the long-haul merchant fleet of the ancient Mediterranean, the largest vessels a Judean would have heard of. This reading names them and, before them, the ships of the sea generally. Some read the pair as preserving two older forms of the same line; either way the effect is that the whole business of sea trade is in the list of things to be brought low.

world_behind.title: Moles and bats
world_behind.text: Verse 20 sends men to throw their gold and silver idols to animals that live underground and in caves. The images cost a fortune and end up where nothing can see them, which is the joke, and the place their owners are also headed by verse 21.

world_behind.title: A reading for a colony with no silver problem
world_behind.text: Nephi's people were building in a new land, not living in a boom. Copying a chapter about the danger of full treasuries was a choice, and it fits the instruction he had just given: liken these words to yourselves. The chapter's subject is not wealth but height, and any people can be high.

words.text: Not unkind. In older usage a mean man is a man of low rank, the ordinary person, set here against "the great man" (v. 9). The pairing covers the whole social ladder in four words, which is the point of using it: the refusal to bow is not a failing of one class. It runs top to bottom.

Height turned into an attitude. The word belongs to a chapter obsessed with elevation, and it is one of a cluster: lofty looks, lifted up, high tower, high mountains. Isaiah does not moralize about pride in the abstract. He builds a vocabulary of tallness and then knocks everything in it down in the same three verses.

A fortification word: walled, defended against attack. Set beside the high tower, it completes a picture of military security. Everything in Isaiah's list of doomed things is something people built to feel safe or grand, and the wall makes the pattern explicit, since a fence exists only because of what is outside it.

A far port, probably in the western Mediterranean, and a byword for distance and cargo. Its ships were the era's largest. In a chapter whose other targets are mountains, cedars, towers, and walls, the fleet is the one item that moves, and it is included to show that mobility is no exemption either.

Height taken as a quality of a person. The word appears twice in this record and twice in the King James Bible, one of each being this verse. Verse 17 pairs it with haughtiness and bows both down. Jacob's allegory uses the other instance of a vineyard, where the loftiness is branches overcoming their own roots (Jacob 5:48), so the record keeps the word for growth that has outrun what holds it up.

Blind burrowers. The idols that were carried in procession get thrown to the animals of the dark, and the choice of creature is precise: what people made to be seen is delivered to something that cannot see. Verse 21 then puts the owners in the same geography, in clefts and ragged rocks.

phrases.term: Yea, come, for ye have all gone astray
phrases.text: The KJV's invitation ends where it starts: "come ye, and let us walk in the light of the LORD" (Isa. 2:5), and the next verse turns abruptly to judgment. This reading adds the missing hinge, an indictment attached to the invitation itself, "every one to his wicked ways" (v. 5). The turn that felt sudden now has a stated cause, and the invitation is issued to people already named as lost.

cites.quote: every one to his wicked ways

spans.text: every one to his wicked ways

phrases.term: Therefore, O Lord, thou hast forsaken thy people
phrases.text: The KJV reads as a statement about God in the third person. Here a vocative is inserted and the sentence becomes prayer: the prophet turns from the people he has just addressed and speaks to God about them. One added phrase changes who is being talked to, and it puts Isaiah in the posture the chapter keeps recommending, looking up rather than around.

phrases.term: The great man humbleth himself not
phrases.text: The chapter's most consequential variant, and it is one word. The KJV has the mean man bowing down and the great man humbling himself, then asks for no forgiveness, which has puzzled readers for centuries. Two inserted negatives resolve it: nobody bows, nobody humbles himself, and the plea against forgiveness follows from the refusal. The verse becomes an argument instead of a difficulty.

phrases.term: O ye wicked ones, enter into the rock
phrases.text: The KJV commands without naming an addressee: "Enter into the rock, and hide thee in the dust" (Isa. 2:10). The addition tells us who is being sent into hiding, and a second addition tells us what happens there, since the glory of his majesty "shall smite thee" (v. 10) rather than merely appearing. In this reading the hiding place is where the blow lands.

phrases.term: The day of the Lord of Hosts soon cometh
phrases.text: The KJV's day "shall be upon every one that is proud" (Isa. 2:12), a description of scope. This version adds timing and reach: soon, and upon all nations, before narrowing to the proud. Nephi is copying for a people who had watched one prophesied destruction arrive on schedule, and the added word about speed would not have read as a figure of speech to them.

phrases.term: All the ships of the sea
phrases.text: Where the KJV lists one fleet, this reading lists two. The named ships of Tarshish keep their place, and ahead of them stands every ship at sea. Whatever produced the doubling, it widens the target from a famous trading fleet to shipping itself, which suits a chapter that has just finished listing every high and fortified thing on land.

Verses 19 and 21 are nearly identical in both texts, and both end with the same pair of nouns. The KJV keeps the order both times, "the glory of his majesty" (Isa. 2:21); this reading reverses it the second time. Small as it is, the swap keeps the refrain from settling into a formula, and it is the sort of variation a listener notices before a reader does.

verses.label: v. 5
verses.title: An invitation gains an accusation
verses.text: Isaiah 2:5 says only "O house of Jacob, come ye, and let us walk in the light of the Lord." Here a clause is added before the walking: "yea, come, for ye have all gone astray, every one to his wicked ways." The verse still invites, but it now states what is being walked away from, and it says all.

verses.label: v. 10
verses.title: The reader is named and threatened inside one verse
verses.text: "Enter into the rock, and hide thee in the dust" gains a vocative, "O ye wicked ones," and a consequence, "shall smite thee." Isaiah's verse describes a fear that comes; this one addresses a person and tells him what will reach him. Fifteen of these twenty-two verses differ from Isaiah 2, and the additions run heavily this way.

verses.label: v. 12–14
verses.title: The day is made to arrive, and made universal
verses.text: Isaiah's "the day of the Lord of hosts shall be upon every one that is proud" becomes a day that "soon cometh upon all nations." Verse 13 gains "the day of the Lord shall come"; verse 14 gains "and upon every people." The variants widen a judgment on the proud of one nation into a judgment on everyone, and do it in three consecutive verses.

verses.label: v. 16
verses.title: One line is added to a list of ships
verses.text: Isaiah 2:16 names the ships of Tarshish and the pleasant pictures. Here a third item comes first: "and upon all the ships of the sea." The King James verse is specific to a trading fleet. The addition makes it every hull afloat, which is the same widening the variants performed on the nations three verses earlier.

verses.label: v. 21
verses.title: A pair of nouns changes places
verses.text: The King James verse has men fleeing "the glory of his majesty"; here it reads the majesty of his glory. Nothing is added or removed, only reversed, and it is the last substantive change in the chapter.

chapter.title: A chapter built on one word
chapter.text: Everything in it is high, lifted up, exalted, lofty, or haughty, and everything but one is brought low. The exception is stated twice in identical words: the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day. The structure is not an argument about pride so much as a demonstration of what happens to height when there is a taller thing.

chapter.title: The variants push toward the second person
chapter.text: Someone is named in verse 5 as having gone astray, someone is addressed in verse 6 as Lord, someone is called wicked in verse 10 and told the glory will smite thee. The KJV's chapter describes; this reading keeps turning to face people. For a prophet copying it out to persuade his brothers, that direction is useful.

chapter.title: The hard verse is resolved rather than smoothed
chapter.text: Verse 9 in the King James reads as a request that the humble not be forgiven, which no translator has been comfortable with. The reading here turns both verbs negative and the difficulty disappears. It is the clearest case in the block of a variant doing interpretive work, and it does the work by changing what the verse says.

chapter.title: The end of the chapter answers its beginning
chapter.text: Verse 2 puts a mountain at the top of the mountains and sends the nations up to it. Verse 22 tells the reader to stop accounting for man, whose breath is in his nostrils. Between them everything else that claimed height is levelled. The chapter is a map of where to direct attention, and it clears the field before pointing.

chapter.title: Why this chapter first
chapter.text: Nephi had thirteen chapters of Isaiah to arrange and began with the one about a house of the Lord established in the last days and a people undone by their own supply. His colony had just built a temple and was starting to prosper. The likening does not need to be spelled out, and he does not spell it out.

chapter.title: The list refuses to end where a reader expects
chapter.text: After cedars and mountains, the natural close would be the works of men, towers and walls. Instead it keeps going to ships and then to pleasant pictures, to art itself. The last item on the list of doomed high things is beauty made for its own sake, and Isaiah does not pause over it.

chapter.title: A day named without a date
chapter.text: The chapter says the day comes soon and comes on all nations, and never says when. That combination governs the whole Isaiah block that follows: near enough to change behavior, unspecified enough that no generation gets to consider itself exempt.

applications.title: Follow the money to the shrine
applications.text: Isaiah's inventory ends where it does on purpose. Trace one line of your own spending over the last year to what it was finally for, and keep asking until the answer names a thing you serve.

applications.title: Find the tower
applications.text: Identify the one structure in your life built mainly so that you feel secure or impressive, a title, a balance, a following. Ask what it would mean for that thing to be brought low, and whether your standing with God changes at all when it goes.

applications.title: Bow before you have to
applications.text: The verse's whole complaint is that nobody, high or low, bows. Choose one place this week where you would normally hold your position and yield instead, to a person, a correction, or a commandment you have been arguing with.

applications.title: Take the invitation with the diagnosis
applications.text: This reading pairs "come and walk in the light" with "ye have all gone astray." Practice receiving both halves at once about yourself, without using the second to disqualify yourself from the first. The verse offers them in that order for a reason.

applications.title: Convert one weapon
applications.text: Swords became plowshares: a capacity for harm became a capacity for food. Name a sharp thing you are good at, an argument style, a memory for slights, and find the one use of it this month that grows something.

applications.title: Stop accounting for a man
applications.text: Pick the person whose opinion currently has more weight in your decisions than it deserves. Do one thing this week you have been postponing because of how they would read it, and notice how small the consequence turns out to be.

questions.text: When did I last go somewhere specifically to be taught God's ways?
What have I been replenished from lately, and would I be comfortable naming the sources out loud?
Where do I refuse to bow, and is the refusal about principle or about position?
What in my life is lofty in a way that could not survive the day this chapter describes?
What have I paid a great deal for that I would be embarrassed to be found holding?
Whose breath am I still counting on, and what would change if I stopped?
